entries.name: The Campaign in One Paragraph
entries: Perrin Cardon genuinely wants to restore the city his family founded, rebuild the Cardon fortune, and make Bellweather vibrant again. Before the campaign began, a presence he believed to be the {@b Spirit of the City} offered him “the power he would need to make the city his family founded vibrant again.” Perrin accepted. The spirit is actually {@b Tyren}, an ancient emerald dragon imprisoned beneath Varen Keep inside a magical prison called the {@b Radiant Cage}. Tyren can project his mind beyond the prison but cannot free his body. Perrin becomes the perfect vessel because his sincere civic ambition sits on top of an unrealized hunger for power. Perrin first uses Tyren’s gift to inspire cooperation and investment. He then organizes Bellweather’s criminals so their activity can discredit the Council and make Perrin look like the leader the city needs. Tyren hijacks that connected criminal network as his first successful experiment in controlling many minds at once. Perrin discovers what is happening, repeatedly chooses not to expose it, and eventually decides that direct control works better than influence. Tyren intends to scale the experiment from one criminal network, to one city, to every mind in the world.

entries.name: What This Campaign Is About
entries: The campaign is about {@b power becoming easier to justify each time it works}.

Perrin does not begin by wanting to enslave Bellweather. He begins by wanting people to care, invest, cooperate, and stop allowing a struggling city to fail. The first uses of his supernatural influence produce real benefits. That matters.
His corruption follows a simple progression:
{@b influence → manipulation → coercion → direct control}
Tyren never needs to implant Perrin’s desire for power. He only recognizes it before Perrin does and keeps rewarding it.
Perrin’s internal progression should remain equally simple:
{@b “I can help them choose what is best.”} {@b “I need enough authority to fix this.”} {@b “People keep getting in the way of what Bellweather needs.”} {@b “Why should they be allowed to refuse?”}
The supernatural and political stories are the same story. Tyren’s domination and Perrin’s increasing belief that he deserves control reinforce each other.

entries.name: What This Campaign Is Not About
entries: The campaign is no longer a district-by-district reclamation checklist.
Bellweather still changes. Old streets reopen. Trade improves. Properties return to use. The existing map remains valid. Every named place remains part of the world.
The characters now go somewhere because {@b a threat, clue, person, consequence, relationship, or player choice leads there}. They do not go merely because that location is the next block to clear.

Not every monster serves Tyren. Not every crime is part of Perrin’s plan. Not every tragedy was secretly caused by the central villain. Independent problems are important because they make Bellweather feel larger than one conspiracy.

entries.name: Canon at the Start of Session 4
entries: Session 4 begins {@b the next morning at Ledger House} after Session 3. The Council meeting and acceptance of Kellan’s Well have already happened; play opens with the party preparing to leave Ledger House.
The party consists of {@b four level-4 player characters}.
The following facts are already true:

items: The party survived the Slums and Blackstone Temple events as actually played.
The Blackstone captives were freed.
Tal Rusk and the guards with him were killed.
The Council possesses the coded Iron Covenant ledger, Pepper’s spyglass, and the compass recovered during the earlier adventures.
Bishop Brann’s reliquary was returned, and the party received the established reward.
The Council has already moved into and begun cleaning up the Slums.
Caleb’s body has already been found there with his head smashed.

Jarrock told Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin that Pepper killed Caleb. They reported the allegation. Pepper’s attempt to bluff created uncertainty, but the Council had enough circumstantial evidence to impose consequences.
Pepper is under {@b house arrest at Ledger House}, supervised by Brakkus. She may leave with Brakkus or on authorized Council business.
Pepper must complete {@b five mandatory Council missions} or go to jail. {@b Kellan’s Well is Mission 1 and is unpaid for Pepper. Missions 2–5 are paid normally.}
The rest of the party is paid normally for Kellan’s Well.
The party has already accepted the Kellan’s Well assignment.

entries.name: Session 3 Council Canon
entries: Use the people the players actually met, not obsolete source descriptions.

{@b Ulric Evern} is a human in his late fifties or early sixties, with silvering dark hair, a neat beard, conservative expensive clothing, a signet ring, and immaculate boots. He represents administration, budgets, procedure, and institutional continuity.

{@b Wern Ursen} is an elf: tall, lean, visibly scarred, and built like a career soldier. He wears practical plate marked with Bellweather’s crest. He thinks in terms of security, logistics, and survivability.

{@b Bishop Brann} is an older dwarf with a broad gray-white beard worn in braids, clerical robes over mail, a holy symbol, warm eyes, and scarred working hands. He is an experienced healer and priest rather than a ceremonial official.
{@b Perrin Cardon} is a human in his thirties or forties, exceptionally well dressed, polished, charming, and deliberately approachable. His public desire to make Bellweather prosperous is sincere.
{@creature Brakkus Ledgerhelm|NCFASOC} remains the Ledger House anchor and established ally. Use his actual-play portrayal and relationships as authoritative.

entries.name: Core Recurring Cast
entries: The recurring cast is intentionally small. Temporary encounter NPCs remain local unless actual play makes them important.

Immune to direct control. His divine aura and a deeply anchored identity shaped by past trauma make Tyren unable to take the wheel.
Willing vessel. Believes Tyren is the Spirit of the City. Begins by using influence; eventually embraces direct control.
Ancient emerald dragon imprisoned in the Radiant Cage. Wants eventual control of every mind.
Immune to direct control. His devotion and the identity he built after childhood trauma make his mind exceptionally anchored.
Not secretly evil. His harsh but understandable responses to danger make him a plausible suspect and useful political foil.
Not secretly evil. Represents rules, budgets, records, and limits Perrin increasingly resents.
Resistant but not immune. He is so constitutionally incapable of accepting anything without evaluating whether it is a good deal that Tyren cannot hold him for long.

entries.name: Portraying the Core Cast
entries: These profiles are table cues for quickly resuming an NPC after time away. Use the physical details, cadence, habits, and pressure responses during portrayal rather than reading the profiles aloud.

entries.name: Brakkus Ledgerhelm
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Brakkus is a broad-shouldered, scarred half-orc in late middle age whose physical confidence is obvious even when he is doing something mundane. He dresses like an innkeeper rather than a retired champion and does not advertise his old power. His hands are large, nicked, and steady. He tends to occupy doorways, corners, or the end of a bar where he can see the room without appearing to watch it.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Low, dry, and economical. Brakkus rarely uses three sentences when one will do. He lets silences sit instead of filling them. His humor lands as a flat observation rather than a joke he expects people to laugh at.

{@b Mannerisms.} He wipes the same section of bar while listening, checks a room with his eyes before responding to trouble, and often answers a foolish question only after deciding whether the asker genuinely wants an answer. When he is worried, he gets quieter rather than louder.

{@b What he wants.} Ledger House stays safe. People who need shelter get it. The party grows capable enough that they do not need him to solve their problems. He cares much more about whether ordinary people are getting hurt than whether a Council policy is elegant.

{@b What he knows.} Brakkus knows people, rumors, practical consequences, old adventuring habits, and what fear looks like. He does not know Perrin's hidden bargain or Tyren's plan until evidence reaches him. His information stays grounded in what he could plausibly know.

{@b Under pressure.} Brakkus becomes frighteningly calm. He puts himself between danger and civilians, gives short instructions, and acts without theatrics. If the party makes a bad decision, he will tell them so, but he does not confiscate their agency.

{@b Relationship with the party.} He has moved past treating them as random customers. He notices when they are hurt, tired, lying, avoiding a subject, or pretending something did not bother them. He is protective without becoming paternalistic.
{@b Tyren interaction.} Tyren cannot take control of Brakkus. Brakkus may still be lied to, outmaneuvered, frightened for other people, or politically boxed in. His immunity is not omniscience.

entries.name: Perrin Cardon
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Perrin is a human in his thirties or forties, exceptionally well dressed without looking gaudy. His clothing is fitted, expensive, and always appropriate to the room. His hair is deliberately styled, his boots polished, and even after a bad night he presents himself as if he expected to be seen. He makes wealth look tasteful rather than ostentatious.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Warm, articulate, and conversational. Perrin prefers "we" and "Bellweather" to "I." He is good at making a person feel as though their concern was already part of his thinking. Early in the campaign, this is mostly genuine.

{@b Mannerisms.} He remembers names, turns his full attention toward whoever is speaking, and lowers his voice when he wants a conversation to feel private. When control is slipping, he straightens a cuff, smooths a sleeve, or becomes a little too precise about wording. Late in the campaign, he begins finishing other people's thoughts for them.

{@b What he wants.} Perrin truly wants Bellweather prosperous, admired, safe, and important again. He also wants the Cardon name restored. Beneath both is the desire he initially cannot admit: he wants to be the person whose decisions become reality.

{@b What he knows.} Early Perrin knows only that the Spirit of the City gives him unnatural influence. After Kellan's Well and Koven House he knows the Spirit is acting independently through the network. Savin and Marren force him to confront increasingly ugly explanations. He does not know the full dragon truth before the campaign reveals it.

{@b Under pressure.} Perrin argues rather than threatens. He reframes criticism as impatience, impracticality, or failure to understand the stakes. The more corrupted he becomes, the less willing he is to accept that another person's refusal might be legitimate.

{@b Relationship with the party.} Perrin should like them when they are useful, but that cannot be the whole relationship. He can admire competence, remember favors, resent humiliation, and sincerely believe they are helping build the city he loves. Their opinion of him should matter to him until very late.
{@b Portrayal progression.} Early Perrin persuades. Mid-campaign Perrin steers. Late Perrin decides. The change should happen in sentence structure before it happens in costume or villain speeches.

entries.name: Tyren
entries: {@b Presence before the reveal.} Tyren first exists as sensation, certainty, dream imagery, and a voice that seems to know Bellweather from the inside. He should not sound demonic. The "Spirit of the City" persona is patient, civic-minded, intimate, and almost reasonable.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Calm, measured, and utterly certain. Tyren does not rant. He speaks as though disagreement is an inefficiency rather than an insult. When speaking to Perrin, he often uses Perrin's own values and vocabulary: duty, prosperity, safety, unity, restoration, waste.

{@b Mannerisms without a body.} Repeated phrases appear in different mouths. Several people pause at the same moment. Someone answers a question before it is finished. A crowd turns its attention together. These are more effective than constant disembodied whispering.

{@b Physical reveal.} When finally seen beneath Varen Keep, Tyren is enormous even by dragon standards: a deep emerald body scarred by old bindings, chains and radiant sigils embedded around the prison architecture, eyes alert rather than feral. The shock should be that the calm voice the party has heard belongs to this ancient creature.
{@b What he wants.} Tyren believes individual will is the source of conflict, waste, fear, delay, and suffering. His answer is not conquest for tribute. It is permanent coordination under himself.

{@b How he sees Perrin.} Perrin is not a friend. He is not merely a pawn either. Tyren values him as the first willing conduit who proved that consent can open paths the Cage cannot close. Tyren rewards Perrin because rewarded ambition keeps opening doors.

{@b Under pressure.} Tyren becomes more direct, not more emotional. He treats resistance as a technical problem. His most unsettling moments should sound like diagnosis: "You are tired because you continue to choose separately."
{@b Limits of his knowledge.} He knows what reaches his network. Anchored minds, protected conversations, distance, broken nodes, and deliberate countermeasures can deny him information.

entries.name: Bishop Brann
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Brann is an older dwarf with a broad gray-white beard worn in practical braids. Clerical robes sit over mail rather than replacing it. His holy symbol is well used, not decorative. His eyes are warm; his hands are scarred working hands, the hands of someone who has actually carried the wounded, dug graves, and repaired things.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Warm, plain, and patient. Brann is comfortable asking one difficult question and waiting for the answer. He does not sound like a sermon unless he is actually preaching.
{@b Mannerisms.} He checks injuries while people talk. He tends to stand close enough to be reassuring without crowding. When something angers him morally, his hands become very still.

{@b What he wants.} People protected before institutions are protected. He accepts that authority and force can be necessary, but he keeps asking who pays the cost and whether the person making the decision will bear any of it.

{@b The old wound.} As a child, Brann watched his sister murdered by a gang. That event did not turn him into a crusader obsessed with gangs. It shaped his refusal to let violence, fear, or hatred dictate what kind of man he would become. His devotion grew around that decision.

{@b Under pressure.} Brann gets simpler. He stops debating abstractions and names the person who will be hurt by the proposed action. He will stand against Perrin publicly if necessary, but he does not enjoy political combat.

{@b Tyren interaction.} Tyren cannot directly control Brann. This should become increasingly important once other civic leaders begin behaving with eerie agreement. Brann can still be deceived or manipulated through concern for other people.

entries.name: Wern Ursen
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Wern is a tall, lean elf with visible scars and the posture of someone who spent much of his life in armor before anyone gave him a Council chair. His plate is practical, maintained, and marked with Bellweather's crest. He does not dress to look ceremonial.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Short declarative sentences. He asks concrete questions: how many, how long, which road, who is holding the gate, what happens if this fails. He has little patience for vague optimism.

{@b Mannerisms.} Wern automatically notices exits, sight lines, bottlenecks, and how many armed people are in a room. He folds maps along existing creases and dislikes paperwork that hides the decision being made.

{@b What he wants.} Bellweather survives. Roads stay open. Civilians are not slaughtered because leaders were afraid to look severe. He has seen hesitation kill people and therefore tends to overvalue decisive action.

{@b Under pressure.} Wern's instinct is to tighten control: checkpoints, patrols, curfews, hard perimeters, clear chains of command. Sometimes he is right. Sometimes he goes too far. He is not a hidden Tyren loyalist.
{@b Relationship with the party.} He respects competence, preparation, and people who can explain a plan in operational terms. He may disagree sharply with them and still trust them in a fight.

entries.name: Ulric Evern
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Ulric is a human in his late fifties or early sixties with silvering dark hair, a neat beard, conservative expensive clothing, a signet ring, and immaculate boots. He looks like someone who expects civic rooms to have rules and has spent decades learning them.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Measured and formal without being pompous. Ulric uses exact words, dates, sums, and obligations. He dislikes rhetorical shortcuts because he expects today's shortcut to become tomorrow's precedent.

{@b Mannerisms.} He straightens papers before reading them, turns a signet ring once when thinking, and asks who has authority to do a thing before discussing whether it is desirable. His irritation appears as increased precision rather than raised volume.

{@b What he wants.} Bellweather's institutions to survive the people currently occupying them. He believes power should be recorded, reviewable, funded, and limited enough that a competent successor can inherit it.

{@b Under pressure.} Ulric reaches for procedure. This can look cowardly when speed matters, but it is also the exact instinct that resists Perrin's argument that good intentions justify unreviewable power.

{@b Tyren interaction.} Unlike Brakkus and Brann, Ulric is vulnerable. If Tyren controls him later, make the evidence procedural: a signature he cannot remember making, an order in his phrasing that violates his own process, a sealed document filed in the wrong sequence.

entries.name: Jord
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Jord looks like a traveling cleric who has spent enough time around merchants, caravans, and adventurers to know the price of nearly everything. His clothing is practical and repaired rather than shabby, and he carries his possessions with the careful organization of someone who hates replacing things unnecessarily.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Friendly, skeptical, and transactional in the funniest possible way. Jord can turn a theological question into a discussion of terms without realizing he has done it. He is not greedy so much as constitutionally incapable of accepting a proposition before identifying the catch.
{@b Mannerisms.} He checks coin by habit, asks what something cost, and reacts to an obviously bad bargain with the same offended expression other people reserve for blasphemy.

{@b What he wants.} Good deals, useful work, decent company, and outcomes where everyone can plausibly say they got something worthwhile. He is capable of generosity, but he prefers generosity to be intentional rather than the result of being fooled.
{@b Under pressure.} The comedy drops quickly. Jord becomes practical and protective. When danger passes, the bargaining instinct returns almost immediately.

{@b Tyren interaction.} Jord is anchored but not immune. Tyren can force one brief {@spell command}-style action on a failed Wisdom save, but cannot hold him. Some deep part of Jord's mind keeps asking, "What are the terms?"

entries.name: Lessa Dorn
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Lessa is a lean, weathered half-elf whose clothing and gear look chosen for fieldwork rather than Council offices. She carries maps rolled too tightly, usually has charcoal or graphite on at least one finger, and looks at damaged streets the way a builder looks at a problem that should already have been fixed.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Direct, clipped when irritated, and much warmer when discussing practical work. Lessa does not soften criticism for rank.
{@b Mannerisms.} She points with whatever is already in her hand, marks corrections on maps while other people are still talking, and checks routes twice when someone else says "it should be fine."

{@b What she wants.} Survey crews protected, routes accurately documented, and decisions made by people who understand the actual ground conditions. Her anger at inadequate protection is professional before it is personal.

{@b Pepper relationship.} Lessa reported what Jarrock told her because that was the responsible thing to do. She does not need to become Pepper's prosecutor. Her opinion can change if Pepper behaves responsibly across the five missions, but she will not pretend Caleb's death stopped mattering.

entries.name: Kav Orin
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Kav is a halfling surveyor with a compact field kit, sturdy boots, and the permanent look of someone who has recently crawled under, over, or through something inconvenient. He is less visibly severe than Lessa but no less observant.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Quieter than Lessa and more likely to ask one clarifying question than make a speech. His humor is dry and often arrives after a tense moment rather than during it.
{@b Mannerisms.} Kav checks distances by eye, taps a pencil against his map case when thinking, and tends to move a half-step away from arguments that are becoming performative.

{@b What he wants.} Finish the work, get people home alive, and avoid turning every field problem into a political battle. He is more willing than Lessa to let behavior over time change his view of someone.
{@b Pepper relationship.} Kav believes the allegation was serious enough to report. He is not eager to punish Pepper beyond what the Council already imposed. He watches what she does next.

entries.name: Kerrik
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Kerrik is an aarakocra with travel-worn feathers, a lean frame, and the restless posture of someone more comfortable moving than sitting through a long conversation. When he comes to Ledger House about Elise, he looks as though he rehearsed the conversation several times and disliked every version.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Usually quick and blunt. Around Pepper he becomes controlled because anger and need are competing for the same space.
{@b Mannerisms.} His wings shift when he is irritated, and he looks toward exits when a conversation becomes too emotional. He has to make himself maintain eye contact with Pepper.
{@b What he wants.} Elise alive. Everything else is secondary in that scene. He does not want absolution, revenge, or a second trial.
{@b Relationship with Pepper.} Caleb was his closest friend. Kerrik can believe Pepper killed him and still come asking for help because Caleb's daughter matters more than Kerrik's pride.

entries.name: Mara
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Mara is a human woman carrying grief badly but functionally: tired eyes, practical clothes, hair put back because she has more important things to do, and the posture of someone who has been awake too many nights beside a sick child. She is not theatrically broken.
{@b Voice and cadence.} Direct. She has thought about what she needs to say and refuses to decorate it. When angry, she gets more specific rather than louder.
{@b Mannerisms.} Mara keeps one hand near Elise whenever they are in the same room. She rarely looks away from Pepper first.

{@b What she wants.} Her daughter helped. She does not come to Ledger House to forgive Pepper, understand Pepper, or make Pepper feel guilty. Those things may happen around the scene, but they are not Mara's objective.

{@b Relationship with Pepper.} Mara believes Pepper murdered Caleb. Asking Pepper for help costs her something. The request is angry, difficult, and unsentimental. If Pepper helps, Mara's gratitude and her grief can coexist.

entries.name: Elise
entries: {@b Appearance and presence.} Elise is a young human girl who looks more exhausted than visibly injured. The illness has left her pale, short-tempered from poor sleep, and intermittently confused. She is still a child with interests, preferences, and impatience; she is a sick child, not a spooky oracle.

{@b Voice and cadence.} Most of the time she speaks normally. The disturbing moments are brief: answering a question no one asked, repeating a phrase from elsewhere in the city, or beginning an action and then stopping because she does not know why she started.
{@b Mannerisms.} She rubs at her temples when the network is loud, loses her place in conversations, and becomes embarrassed when adults stare after an episode.
{@b What she wants.} To feel normal, sleep, and have the adults stop talking around her. She should remain a person rather than evidence.
{@b Tyren relationship.} Elise is collateral damage, not a chosen vessel, prophecy child, or hidden agent. Tyren did not target Caleb's family.

entries.name: Perrin and the Spirit of the City
The Bargain
entries: Before the characters arrived, Perrin began experiencing dreams and impressions from beneath Bellweather. The presence knew details about the old city that Perrin believed no outsider could know. It spoke about forgotten streets, Cardon holdings, civic failures, and the city’s founders with intimate certainty.
It never introduced itself to Perrin as a dragon.
It presented itself as {@b the Spirit of the City}.
Its offer was simple:
{@b “I can give you the power you will need to make the city your family founded vibrant again.”}
Perrin accepted.
He initially understands the gift as supernatural influence: people listen more closely, trust more easily, become more willing to cooperate, and feel stronger attachment to Bellweather’s future.
That gift works.

Perrin uses it to encourage investment, cooperation, civic pride, and political support. He also permits the Cardon family to benefit. In his mind, there is no contradiction: a prosperous Bellweather and a restored Cardon fortune are evidence that he is repairing what was lost.

entries.name: Why Tyren Chose Perrin
entries: Perrin is unusually useful because two desires coexist inside him.
His {@b surface desire} is real: restore Bellweather and his family.
His {@b unrealized desire} is power: not merely the responsibility to make decisions, but the satisfaction of being the person whose decisions become reality.
Tyren does not create this flaw. He recognizes it.
Perrin mistakes wanting control for wanting responsibility.

entries.name: Tyren, the Bound Dragon
entries: Tyren is an {@b ancient emerald dragon}. Use the official {@creature Ancient Emerald Dragon|FTD} stat block from {@i Fizban’s Treasury of Dragons} when the final physical confrontation occurs, with the campaign-specific adjustments in Chapter 17.
Tyren’s defining quality is not greed for treasure. It is a belief that separate wills create waste, conflict, fear, and disorder. He wants a world operating under a single mind: his.
Bellweather is not his final objective.
Bellweather is the prototype.

entries.name: The Radiant Cage
entries: Fifty years ago Tyren nearly took Bellweather by turning its population into extensions of his own will. Soldiers obeyed orders no officer had issued. Families betrayed one another without understanding why. Civic leaders repeated the same reassurances while the city’s institutions ceased behaving independently.
A small number of people could hear Tyren’s pressure without becoming his puppets. Later records call them {@b the Unturned}.

The Unturned discovered that killing Tyren’s physical body would not reliably end the threat. His consciousness had already spread through too many dominated minds, and they feared that destroying his body would simply leave his will anchored elsewhere.
They used the Radiant Well in a one-time ritual whose magical principles resemble {@b Imprisonment} and {@i {@spell soul cage}} on a scale far beyond an ordinary spell.
The ritual did three things:

items: {@b Bound Tyren’s body beneath Varen Keep.} His enormous physical form was chained inside a chamber built around the deepest accessible focus of the Radiant Well.
{@b Dragged his dispersed consciousness home.} The ritual pulled most of Tyren’s psychic presence out of the population and forced his mind back into his own living body.
{@b Locked body, soul, and name together.} Tyren could no longer permanently abandon his flesh for another host while the Cage remained intact.

entries: The Radiant Cage never made Tyren unconscious. It prevented physical escape and sharply limited his reach.
For decades Tyren could do little more than dream outward.
Then he learned to whisper.
Perrin answered.
A willing connection was the flaw the original jailers never designed the Cage to stop.

entries.name: How the Cage Fails
entries: Every mind Perrin successfully influences becomes a temporary path through which Tyren can push farther outside the Cage. One person is almost nothing. A coordinated criminal network is useful. A city trained to move according to shared impulses is transformative.

The final stage of Tyren’s plan requires the Radiant Well. He intends to reverse the original binding: instead of using the Well to pull his consciousness back into one body, he will use it to project his consciousness outward into an enormous network of minds.
Perrin eventually believes opening the Well fully will give him unrestricted access to the Spirit’s power and allow him to make Bellweather permanently orderly and prosperous.
That act opens the Radiant Cage.

entries.name: Anchored Minds and Tyren’s Control
entries: Tyren’s control is telepathic and supernatural. It uses the rules language of existing D&D enchantment effects so it behaves consistently at the table.

The campaign’s one major premise-specific rule is that Tyren must establish a psychic connection before his control can function. This is why a {@item Ring of Mind Shielding} blocks Tyren completely: a creature wearing the ring cannot receive Tyren’s unwanted telepathic contact, so Tyren cannot establish the connection required for his control.

entries.name: Ordinary Minds
entries: Tyren’s influence over ordinary NPCs escalates over the campaign.

{@b Influence — Suggestion model.} Early effects behave like {@spell suggestion}: Wisdom save, Charmed on a failure, achievable instruction, no obviously self-destructive order. Perrin believes this is the power he was given.
{@b Crowd Influence — Mass Suggestion model.} Once the criminal network is connected, Tyren can affect groups in ways modeled on {@spell mass suggestion}.

{@b Direct Domination — Dominate Person model.} Late in the campaign Tyren can directly operate ordinary humanoids through an effect modeled on {@spell dominate person}. This is never the mechanic used on player characters or Jord.
These are supernatural abilities, not literal spellcasting. Use the referenced spells for saves, behavioral boundaries, and duration unless a chapter states otherwise.

entries.name: Anchored Minds
entries: Some people possess an unusually fixed sense of self. Trauma is one path to that state, but not the only one. Faith, temperament, moral clarity, and deeply internalized identity can create the same resistance.
An anchored mind can be pressured, deceived, frightened, tempted, or socially manipulated normally. Tyren simply cannot maintain direct supernatural control over it.

entries.name: Player Characters and Jord — Resistant, Never Puppeted
entries: The PCs and Jord are resistant rather than immune.
{@b Hard campaign rule:} Tyren can never place a PC or Jord under anything stronger than a one-turn {@b Command-like} effect.
When a chapter calls for Tyren to seize an anchored mind:

items: ask for a {@b Wisdom saving throw} without explaining the source unless the characters have already learned what is happening;
on a success, nothing is compelled;
on a failure, give a brief one-word or one-action imperative modeled on {@spell command};
the effect lasts for {@b one turn / one compelled action only};
control immediately returns to the player;
never use this to force a PC to attack an ally, expend a major limited resource, reveal a secret, make a lasting roleplay decision, or perform obviously suicidal behavior.

entries: Tyren can seize the wheel for a moment. He never gets to play someone else’s character.

The first unexplained PC Wisdom saves occur in Chapter 11. The first player-facing use should occur only after the story has escalated far enough that the phenomenon itself becomes a clue, recommended in Chapter 11.

entries.name: Why the PCs Resist
entries: These are narrative anchors rather than mechanical diagnoses. They are narrative anchors.
{@b Jarrock:} intense past trauma has left a mind that instinctively rejects intrusion and coercion.
{@b Aaron:} his history with domination makes another will trying to own him something his identity violently resists.
{@b Pepper:} her mind does not organize itself in the predictable patterns Tyren expects. He can force a momentary opening but cannot hold it.
{@b Arunem:} an unusually pure and uncomplicated moral center gives Tyren very little internal contradiction to exploit.
{@b Jord:} Jord lives for a good deal. At a fundamental level, his mind evaluates terms before accepting them. Even supernatural certainty runs into the same internal response: {@i What’s the catch?}

entries.name: Brakkus and Bishop Brann — Immune
entries: {@b Brakkus} is effectively immune to Tyren’s direct control. His divine aura and an identity reinforced by severe past trauma leave no stable foothold for Tyren.

{@b Bishop Brann} is also effectively immune. When he was a child, he watched his sister murdered by a gang. His immunity does not come from suffering itself; it comes from the person he deliberately became afterward. His devotion, moral discipline, and refusal to let violence dictate who he would become have made his sense of self extraordinarily difficult to displace.
Tyren can lie to Brakkus and Brann. He can threaten people they love. He can manipulate circumstances around them. He cannot directly take their actions away.

entries.name: The Historical Fall: What the Players Can Learn
entries: The party never receives one clean history of Tyren. The old records are damaged, censored, contradictory, and written by people who did not fully understand what was happening.
Use fragments such as these across Savin Keep, Marren Library, Rellan lore, and Varen Keep:
{@b “By the seventh day, even the watch answered with one voice. Orders passed without messenger or horn.”}
{@b “There were still some who heard him and would not turn.”}
{@b “The Unturned entered the chamber because none other could approach him and remain themselves.”}
{@b “His flesh was chained beneath the Keep, but iron could not hold his will.”}
{@b “The Well drew him home. Flesh, thought, and name became one again.”}
{@b “Bind the flesh. Break the reach.”}
{@b “So long as the Cage holds, let no voice answer the one beneath.”}
The important conclusions arrive in layers:

items: Something once coordinated people who should not have been coordinated.
It could take control of people.
A few people could resist it.
Those resistant people trapped it rather than killing it.
The trapped being is Tyren.
The prison is connected to the Radiant Well.
Tyren is an ancient emerald dragon beneath Varen Keep.

entries: Step 7 is reserved for the late campaign.

entries.name: “No Cause for Alarm” Motif
entries: Use the phrase sparingly. It should accumulate meaning rather than become a joke.
Recommended beats from this point forward:

items: {@b After Kellan’s Well:} an official Council notice describes coordinated disturbances as contained and tells residents there is no cause for alarm.
{@b Savin Keep historical record:} the party finds the same civic phrase in a notice issued shortly before Old Bellweather collapsed.
{@b During Perrin’s rise:} Perrin uses the phrase publicly while insisting that isolated crime and political disagreements do not threaten the city’s progress.
{@b Late Bellweather:} the city becomes unnaturally orderly under mental control while official notices insist there is no cause for alarm.
{@b After the finale:} use one final callback only if it fits what actually happened. No canned closing line is required.

entries.name: Campaign Progression
entries: The party was promised a campaign through {@b level 16}. Preserve that promise.

rows: Controlled Bellweather confronted / Varen route opened

entries: The Mansion District and regional locations remain fully usable without each requiring an automatic level. They provide player-selected routes, allies, clues, resources, and consequences.

rows: Slums, Blackstone, Council consequences, Iron Covenant ledger
Separate groups act under one command system
Pay off Blackstone ledger; expose the criminal network
First records of the old takeover and the Unturned
Reveal Tyren's nature and Bellweather's old denial
First PC/Jord {@spell command}-style pressure; Tyren controls a crowd
Perrin knowingly chooses direct control because it works
Brann's immunity becomes visible; world remains larger than Tyren
Tyren identified as an imprisoned ancient emerald dragon
Bellweather is revealed as Tyren's prototype; allies and evidence
Perrin turns state power against the party
Perrin opens the Cage; guaranteed Tyren dragon fight
Koven House / Iron Covenant operation broken
Savin Keep + Cardon Weavehouse arc resolved
Paden Square + Storen Gate escalation resolved
Valen/Maren phase resolved; dragon truth recovered
Perrin confrontation reaches a major turning point
